jukan-nand-sandisk-lta-bearish-pushback:
## What actually got sold cheap
NAND holds the photos on your phone and the files on your laptop.
It keeps them with the power off,
and Meta stacks it in data centres.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/USB_flash_drive.JPG/500px-USB_flash_drive.JPG|The USB stick in your drawer. The storage chip inside it is NAND.|Wikimedia Commons|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:USB_flash_drive.JPG

NAND types differ by bits per storage cell.
TLC holds three, QLC holds four.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Cell_types_SLC-PLC_in_comparison_20211102.svg/1280px-Cell_types_SLC-PLC_in_comparison_20211102.svg.png|Bits per cell, side by side. Third from the left is TLC, fourth is QLC.|Wikimedia Commons|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cell_types_SLC-PLC_in_comparison_20211102.svg

More bits per cell means more storage per area, so unit cost falls.
The cell also wears faster and runs slower.

QLC is the cheap end, TLC the durable one.
QLC is the one in question.

## Why sign below the going rate
A long-term agreement, or LTA, fixes volume and price years ahead.

Think of it as a phone contract.
Lock in for two years, the monthly bill drops.
The buyer promises volume, the seller shaves the price.
The fab stays busy, so both sides want it.

An LTA below the spot rate is the normal outcome, not a warning.
SanDisk plans to fill over half its shipments this way, which tilts it further.

## So is $0.38 actually cheap
SanDisk opened near $0.50 a unit, expensive for QLC and close to TLC money.

The deal settled near $0.38, a 24% cut.
@@REF@@SanDisk secures Meta NAND supply deal (Yahoo Finance, 2026-07-24)|https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/sandisk-sndk-secures-meta-nand-171417598.html|https://media.zenfs.com/en/simply_wall_st__316/4ede54afa2108a12bdee07c0b0d94a59

@@CMP@@The bear read|A 24% cut from $0.50 to $0.38. You do not discount that hard on something that sells itself.|Jukan's read|$0.50 was TLC money to begin with. $0.38 is closer to fair, and the LTA took the rest.

Same number, opposite readings, depending on where you set the baseline.

## Is the China story a demand signal
One more story props up the bear case, from China.

Module makers there were reportedly turned away selling enterprise SSDs at home.
A module maker buys NAND chips and assembles them into drives.
@@REF@@Chinese memory vendors pick homegrown YMTC and CXMT over Samsung and Micron (Tom's Hardware, 2026-06-17)|https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/ram/chinese-memory-vendors-snub-industry-giants-in-favor-of-homegrown-ram-chips-samsung-micron-and-sk-hynix-face-a-chinese-supply-chain-revolt|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/tn9gFjhWREg7FV67sMTNJY-2560-80.jpg

Jukan places the cause elsewhere.
Those clouds already buy direct from YMTC, China's own NAND maker.

No reason for a middleman differs from nothing to buy.

## Is an LTA only a safe card
Jukan treats SanDisk filling half its shipments with LTAs as a bull point.
Turn it over and it becomes a cost.

With half the volume fixed years out,
a rise in NAND prices cannot reach it.

An LTA is a floor when prices fall and a ceiling when they climb.
The more bullish on memory, the less appealing a company that pre-sold half its output.

The spread of LTAs is also hard to read as weakness.
Intel and AMD are reportedly signing CPU LTAs with Chinese customers.

Ibiden is the Japanese maker of substrates that package advanced chips.
When Samsung sought them,
Ibiden reportedly asked for LTA guarantees.

That is the buyer locking supply down.
@@REF@@Intel and AMD to sign CPU LTAs with Chinese customers (Serenity, 2026-07-23)|https://x.com/aleabitoreddit/status/2080153334888182065

## What the next two days did
Two days later the market moved the other way.

On the 27th SanDisk fell over 14% in a session,
47% below its June 22 high.
About $170 billion of market value went in a month.

None of that proves Jukan wrong on how the contract was priced.
It does say the market reads this as the cycle, not the contract.
@@REF@@SanDisk drops 14% in a day, 47% off its June high (The Kobeissi Letter, 2026-07-27)|https://x.com/KobeissiLetter/status/2081814364928057486

## What settles it
The question comes down to one thing.
Did the discount come from the contract, or from the cycle turning?
If it is the contract, this drop can reverse.
If it is the cycle, it has further to run.

Two things will tell.

If next quarter's QLC contract prints above $0.38, Jukan's read holds.
If below, $0.38 was a starting point, not a floor.

And if SanDisk's LTA share clears half,
there will be a stretch where NAND rises and this name lags.

Either way, a company with half its volume at fixed prices
rises less on the way up and sinks less on the way down.
That asymmetry comes before the direction call.
jukan-cxmt-3d-ic-niche-strategy: The chip industry's race to boost AI performance is shifting from process shrinks to 3D stacking, which fuses logic and memory in one package, and Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are staying cautious about commercializing it while China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) moves to claim the niche, semiconductor analyst Jukan reports. Samsung's foundry division is reportedly fielding a steady stream of inquiries about 3D ICs as demand grows for custom AI chips like ASICs and inference chips alongside Nvidia's general-purpose GPUs. Industry officials say custom, 3D-stacked DRAM is a fundamentally different business from the standardized, mass-produced DRAM that Samsung and SK hynix are built around, since every customer wants a different memory configuration and stacking method, making it hard to run profitably at scale. That is why the two Korean giants are expected to keep 3D IC work at the research stage rather than mobilizing full business units, while later entrants chasing niche demand move first. CXMT, blocked from the high-bandwidth memory market by US export controls, is reportedly building 3D IC capability instead, and Taiwan's Winbond is named alongside it as another niche player. CXMT has reportedly already produced several 3D DRAM sample chips ahead of rivals worldwide.
kobeissi-margin-debt-net-credit-record: A fresh sign of investors piling into stocks with borrowed money rather than cash has emerged. According to The Kobeissi Letter, net credit balances, the cash investors hold in brokerage accounts minus margin debt (money borrowed against stock holdings), fell $70 billion in June to a record negative $1.06 trillion. A negative reading means investors collectively owe more than they hold in cash. That deficit has more than quadrupled since the 2022 bear market, over which time margin debt itself climbed $895 billion to a record $1.50 trillion. Kobeissi contrasts this with the 2008 financial crisis, when net credit balances stayed positive, meaning investors held more cash than debt amid a broad flight from risk into safety. The current numbers point the opposite way, with Kobeissi describing investor risk appetite as being at unprecedented levels.
jukan-korea-memory-mega-mou-950b: SK hynix agreed to supply $750 billion (about 1,085 trillion won) worth of advanced memory chips to Nvidia and other US tech giants over the next five years, according to Kim Yong-beom, South Korea's presidential chief of staff for policy, relayed by chip-industry commentator Jukan on X. The same day, Samsung Electronics signed a separate memorandum of understanding with Broadcom covering $200 billion (about 290 trillion won) in advanced memory supply and foundry cooperation for AI chip production, also over five years. Both announcements came during President Lee Jae-myung's visit to Silicon Valley, where South Korean officials have been framing the trip as a showcase for the country's memory chip industry. The SK hynix deal spans Nvidia and unnamed other technology companies, while the Samsung-Broadcom MOU pairs memory supply with foundry work, since Broadcom designs custom AI chips for clients like Google and Meta that need a manufacturing partner. Around the same time, Anthropic's chief executive said separately that the company had signed its own supply agreements with both Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, adding a third major AI buyer to the mix. The deals come as demand for memory from AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic has surged all at once, with Samsung and SK hynix each pursuing large customers in the race for high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, market share. The figures are large enough to raise questions about how binding they are. Both are framed as five-year memorandums rather than signed, itemized contracts, so how much of the $950 billion combined total converts into actual revenue depends on terms still being worked out.
jukan-apple-micron-china-memory-lobbying: Apple is lobbying the White House to allow Chinese-made memory chips in its products, according to the Wall Street Journal, as memory prices used in iPhones have surged this year. Micron, the US memory chipmaker, is reportedly pushing back hard, arguing the exemption should never be granted. Chip-industry commentator Jukan, writing on X, disputed Apple's stated reasoning. Apple has argued that rising memory costs are an inflation problem that forces it to raise iPhone prices, but Jukan calculated that a roughly fivefold jump in memory prices added only about $50 to Apple's per-unit cost, while Apple raised iPhone prices by $250, a gap he says undercuts the inflation argument and points instead to margin protection. Jukan also referenced Apple's practice in 2023 of buying NAND flash memory near cost and reselling it to consumers at what he described as a 90% margin, calling the move vicious, and said Micron chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra has held a grudge against Apple dating back to his time as a SanDisk co-founder. The dispute comes as Chinese memory makers YMTC and CXMT have been rapidly gaining NAND and DRAM market share, so if Apple does expand its use of Chinese chips, it could also weaken the pricing power of US memory makers including Micron. Those characterizations and anecdotes are Jukan's own framing rather than independently confirmed reporting, though the underlying WSJ account of the lobbying dispute between Apple and Micron is sourced reporting.
semianalysis-amd-cuda-moat-advancing-ai-:
SemiAnalysis has raised AMD's odds of catching Nvidia from a flat 0% to what it now calls a great chance. It is a paid research shop that digs deep on semiconductors, and it has been especially hard on AMD's software. That such a shop changed its mind is the heart of this piece.
But it is worth reading why the same piece says it is still early.

## What changed its mind?
Two things drove the upgrade: the chip and the customers.
AMD's new MI455X accelerator is the first datacenter chip built on TSMC's 2-nanometer process.
It stacks HBM4 memory 12 high for 432 gigabytes per package, more than the 8 stacks and 288 gigabytes Nvidia and Google use.

@@CHK@@MI455X HBM4|432GB, 12 stacks|Nvidia & Google|288GB, 8 stacks|FP8 compute|20 petaflops@@On memory capacity and process node, AMD genuinely leads. The spec edge is real. But the two risks SemiAnalysis flags are about production and software, not specs, so these numbers alone don't settle it.@@Checked 2026-07-27 · AMD Advancing AI 2026 (2026-07-25) · NVIDIA public specs

The customers showed up too. Anthropic committed to 2 gigawatts of AMD chips, and AMD answered with an equity investment of up to 5 billion dollars in Anthropic.
Microsoft, which had dropped AMD after quality problems, reversed course and will bring the new racks into its cloud. The end user is expected to be OpenAI.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_%283706444821%29.jpg/960px-Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_%283706444821%29.jpg|A rack of GPUs in a datacenter. AMD's new Helios rack ties 72 GPUs into a single unit.|Wikimedia Commons|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_(3706444821).jpg

@@REF@@Microsoft will deploy AMD's Helios rack at scale on Azure (Tom's Hardware, 2026-07-20)|https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/microsoft-will-deploy-amds-helios-rack-scale-ai-accelerator-at-scale-on-azure-radeon-instinct-mi455x-and-epyc-venice-power-will-be-available-through-redmonds-cloud-infrastructure|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/KVDkgSDu7PnDSMSF4P8fX4-1920-80.jpg

## So why only a 'chance'?
The headline and the body don't line up. That gap is the point of this card.

@@CMP@@What the headline says|From 0% to a great chance of success. AMD is finally challenging Nvidia's software moat.|What the same body says|Its key automated-test parity is still at 0%, and the 90% target was missed and pushed to October.

SemiAnalysis flags two risks.
One is rack production. Early Helios units hit reliability problems in the backplane, so the ramp is slow.
The other is heavier. AMD is chronically short of the in-house GPUs it needs to build and automatically test its software. SemiAnalysis writes that it has a single-digit multiple fewer than Nvidia.
With too little test hardware, the pass rate that shows whether the software is verified to Nvidia's level lags behind.

## Don't good specs settle it?
The same shop's own measurements from months ago point the other way.
In a February 2026 inference benchmark, SemiAnalysis said AMD's earlier chip was completely beaten by Nvidia's B200 on low-precision (FP4) disaggregated inference. On open-source distributed inference, it said AMD trailed by more than six months.
A spec-sheet lead and measured performance are still two different stories.

@@REF@@AMD to supply Anthropic with 2 gigawatts of Instinct MI450 GPUs (Tom's Hardware, 2026-07-22)|https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/amd-to-supply-anthropic-with-2-gigawatts-of-instinct-mi450-gpus|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/iAtJT6Ab8gPu3iDZq9bCnL-1920-80.jpg

## How is this different from the last card?
If the Jukan card views the same CUDA-moat debate from the DeepSeek and Huawei side, this one views it from AMD's side.
Both say the software wall is getting lower. What is honest about this piece is that it stakes its conclusion on execution, not specs.
Adding memory and lining up customers is done. What is left is verifying the software that runs on top to Nvidia's level, and that won't be settled until after October.
meru-treasury-yield-deficit-not-just-oil: Rising oil prices explain only part of the Treasury yield spike, Korean investment blogger Meru argues, the bigger driver is a structural mismatch between how much debt Washington needs to sell and how much the market wants to buy. The 10-year yield broke above 4.7% intraday, and most coverage blames it on crude, since the Strait of Hormuz is blocked again and Houthi attacks threaten the Red Sea. Oil does feed into inflation broadly, through gasoline, plastics, fertilizer and power generation costs, but breakeven inflation, the rate implied by inflation-protected Treasuries, has barely moved, sitting around 2.3% for both 10 and 30-year debt. Instead, the 30-year real yield has climbed to its highest since the 2008 financial crisis, meaning borrowing itself has simply gotten more expensive. Meru traces that to Treasury supply and demand: the market has grown from $4.5 trillion in 2007 to $31 trillion today, China has flipped from buyer to net seller in favor of gold, Japanese investors sold $29.6 billion of Treasuries net in Q1 2026, and the Fed keeps shrinking its balance sheet. Washington's annual interest bill has topped $1.2 trillion, the FY2026 deficit is projected near $2.07 trillion, and a Supreme Court ruling against IEEPA tariffs forced billions in refunds that analysts say adds roughly $180 billion a year to the deficit through 2036. Big Tech is competing for the same buyers too: global corporate bond issuance hit a record $3.68 trillion in the first half of 2026, led by Amazon's $54 billion, forcing the Treasury to offer richer yields to compete for pension and insurance money.
serenity-aaoi-pluggables-cpo-coexist:
The debate over whether co-packaged optics (CPO) will soon make traditional pluggable optical transceivers obsolete in AI data centers got a reality check this week. Analyst Serenity relayed comments from a photonics-industry CEO, made on an industry podcast called "Market Insights: Photonics & AI," arguing pluggables have roughly another decade of relevant life left, not months.

The exchange started with a reader asking whether Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) is in trouble as CPO, which mounts optical modules directly next to a processor's chip package instead of plugging them in at the edge of a server, gains traction. Serenity's answer: not exactly. AAOI is also developing CPO technology, it's simply further behind on commercializing it than some peers, so lagging on one architecture doesn't mean the company is being left out of the market entirely.

## Why CPO doesn't kill pluggables overnight
The CEO's broader framework, as relayed, is that the industry is heading toward multiple coexisting architectures rather than one clean winner. Alongside pluggables and CPO, a newer category called near-package optics (NPO), which sits closer to the chip than a pluggable but doesn't go as far as full co-packaging, is described as a major opportunity over the next five years. That means capital and R&D spending across the optical supply chain is spreading across at least three architectures rather than concentrating on CPO alone.

@@CMP@@Common read|CPO will soon make pluggable transceivers obsolete as AI clusters scale up.|Industry insider's read|Pluggables stay commercially relevant for roughly a decade, coexisting with CPO and NPO rather than one winning outright.

The binding constraint across all three paths, per the CEO, isn't architecture choice but manufacturing capacity and raw material availability, likely a reference to the industry's tight supply of continuous-wave (CW) lasers used to power optical modules. That suggests demand for optical components is outrunning the industry's ability to build them, regardless of which technology wins.

This is secondhand color from a podcast relayed through a tweet, not a company roadmap or earnings guidance, so it should be read as directional industry sentiment rather than a confirmed timeline for AAOI or any single supplier.
kobeissi-m2-outpaces-gdp-g7: Money creation keeps outpacing real economic growth across the G7, a fresh set of figures shows. According to The Kobeissi Letter, Canada's M2 money supply (a measure of cash, checking deposits and savings-type accounts) has grown 368% since January 2004, the largest increase among G7 economies, while the Canadian economy expanded just 159% in nominal terms over the same period. The US shows a similar gap, with M2 up 279% against 171% nominal GDP growth. France's M2 has surged 258% and the eurozone's 211%, both far outpacing nominal growth of 84% and 102% respectively. Japan is the outlier in the other direction, with M2 up only 90% since 2004, but its economy grew just 25% over that span, the slowest pace in the G7. Kobeissi frames this as a widening gap between how fast money is being created and how fast economies are actually growing.
trump-xi-putin-no-weapons-iran: President Trump said both Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin personally assured him they will not sell weapons to Iran, a claim that, if it holds, would cut off two of the countries most capable of arming Tehran as its war grinds into its fifth month. Trump wrote on Truth Social that Xi made the pledge at their recent meeting in Beijing and said it extends to Chinese companies as well, not just the government. He framed the assurance as tied to the broader US-China relationship, saying he is doing Xi "very big favors" in return. On Putin, Trump said the Russian leader made a similar commitment despite the ongoing war in Ukraine, where Russia's relationship with the US continues alongside its ties to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Trump drew a distinction with his own weapons sales, saying the US sells arms to NATO countries rather than directly to Ukraine, and that what those countries do with the weapons afterward is not something he tracks. He added that any weapons flow from China or Russia to Iran would be "very bad for them," without elaborating on what response that might trigger. The statement comes as Iran has already rejected a US-backed ceasefire proposal from Iraqi mediators, and as oil and shipping routes near the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea remain under pressure from the conflict. Neither Beijing nor Moscow has publicly confirmed Trump's account of the conversations.
jukan-amd-mi500-tam-14t: Semiconductor analyst Jeff Pu has raised his forecast for the AI accelerator market to $1.4 trillion by 2030, up from an earlier $1 trillion estimate, and now expects the market to already reach $1 trillion by 2028, according to a note relayed by chip-industry commentator Jukan on X. Pu's note, focused on AMD's AI roadmap, also lifted the server CPU total addressable market to more than $220 billion by 2030, with agentic AI workloads expected to make up roughly half of that demand and the ratio of CPUs to GPUs in data centers tightening toward 1:1. On AMD's own hardware, Pu highlighted the MI455X accelerator as a major step up from its predecessor, the MI355X, citing 34 times higher throughput and 18 times lower cost per generated token, and said it already beats Nvidia's B200 chip on some large language model inference workloads. Looking further out, Pu said AMD's next-generation MI500 chip will bring optical interconnects, a faster way of linking chips together using light instead of electrical signals, putting it ahead of Nvidia's upcoming Rubin Ultra chip in areas like high-bandwidth memory, four-die packaging, and how many chips can be linked into a single system. He also flagged AMD's Venice server CPU as the strongest option for AI workloads, with 2 to 2.2 times higher throughput than competing chips, and estimated around 300,000 CoWoS advanced packaging units will be built for AMD in 2027, which would lift the average price AMD can charge per chip. Pu kept his price target and estimates unchanged despite the upgraded market forecasts.
kobeissi-equity-etf-record-880b: US equity ETFs have pulled in $880 billion in new money so far this year, already the second-largest annual haul on record after only the all-time high set in 2025, and on pace to blow past that record before year-end, according to data highlighted by The Kobeissi Letter. The current pace of inflows is more than double what the market saw at the same point in both 2021 and 2025, two years that themselves ranked among the strongest on record for equity fund flows. If inflows keep coming in at this rate, Kobeissi estimates the full-year total could top $1.4 trillion, roughly $500 billion above the roughly $920 billion record set in 2025. The scale of buying stands out given how choppy the past week has been for stocks. The S&P 500 gave back a full day's gains and closed lower on Thursday as the Iran war escalated, and Intel's post-earnings rally evaporated within days, wiping out about $90 billion in market value. Investors pulling back from individual stocks or single-day swings evidently haven't pulled back from US equities as an asset class overall, at least not yet. Whether that gap between headline-driven day-to-day selling and steady underlying inflows can keep holding as the Iran conflict grinds into its fifth month is an open question the market hasn't had to answer yet.
kobeissi-intel-erases-rally: Intel's stock has erased its entire post-earnings rally, falling 4% on Thursday after surging as much as 15% following Tuesday's blowout second-quarter report, The Kobeissi Letter reports. The reversal has wiped out roughly $90 billion in market capitalization since the rally peaked around 4:20 p.m. ET the day after earnings. Intel had posted its strongest quarterly revenue growth in more than fifteen years on Tuesday, with the Data Center and AI segment up 59% to $6.3 billion, sending shares up double digits in the days that followed. But the gains proved short-lived. The pullback comes as broader market volatility rose Thursday, with the S&P 500 also giving back its gains as the Iran war escalated and technology stocks fell across the board, muddying the read on whether Intel's retreat reflects specific doubts about the earnings quality or simply a risk-off day for the whole market. Intel's GAAP results still showed an $11 billion net loss driven by one-time charges even as adjusted profit swung positive, a split that some investors may be revisiting now that the initial excitement has faded. The stock remains up from where it started the week, but the speed of the reversal shows how quickly gains tied to a single earnings beat can unwind once the market has time to sit with the details.
kobeissi-sp500-iran-war-selloff: The S&P 500 gave back its entire daily gain and closed lower on Thursday, as an escalation in the Iran war triggered a broad pullback in technology stocks, The Kobeissi Letter reports. The index had been trading in positive territory earlier in the session before reversing course, a move Kobeissi tied directly to the intensifying conflict, now in its 145th day after Iran rejected a US-brokered ceasefire proposal put forward by Iraqi mediators. The reversal landed on a day already crowded with unsettling cross-currents for markets. Intel's post-earnings rally evaporated, wiping out roughly $90 billion in market value, and the 30-day correlation between AI infrastructure stocks and the semiconductor index had separately collapsed toward zero, the lowest in more than four and a half years. Taken together, the day's price action suggests investors are growing more selective and more nervous at the same time, willing to sell first and ask questions later when geopolitical risk resurfaces, even against a backdrop of record equity ETF inflows earlier in the year. Oil and Treasury markets have already been carrying a war-risk premium for months, and a longer, more uncertain conflict raises the odds that equity markets start pricing in the same risk more persistently, rather than treating each escalation as a one-day scare.
serenity-googl-waymo-uber-split: Uber and Google's self-driving unit Waymo may be headed for a split, the Financial Times reported, according to investor commentary account Serenity, who says the shift confirms a view held for over a year. Serenity had argued that Uber's partnership with Waymo was a mistake from the start, since it effectively turned Uber into a distribution channel Google could use to scale its own robotaxi service before eventually competing directly. In Serenity's view, that risk has essentially been realized: Waymo, now positioned as Uber's own partner, looks set to become one of its most serious disruptors in ride-hailing. Serenity had previously flagged that other neutral players, such as Nebius's Avride, or a fully vertically integrated approach, would have made more sense for Uber's long-term positioning than tying its distribution to a company with its own robotaxi ambitions. The report adds a new wrinkle to how investors read Alphabet's self-driving bet: rather than a side project, Waymo increasingly looks like a business Alphabet could operate on its own terms, independent of the ride-hailing incumbents it once needed for scale. For Uber, the question shifts from whether Waymo helps fill its network to whether Waymo eventually competes with it directly for the same riders.
kobeissi-datacenter-power-2035: US data center electricity demand is projected to jump 253% from 2026 levels to a record 194 gigawatts by 2035, The Kobeissi Letter reports, a figure roughly equal to the output of 194 traditional nuclear reactors. As a result, data centers are expected to account for about 20% of total US electricity consumption by 2035, up from roughly 6% today, with the share already projected to hit 12% by 2030. Much of the buildout is concentrated in a handful of grid regions, chief among them PJM, the interconnection that serves Washington DC and 13 states including Virginia, Pennsylvania and Ohio, where AI data center clusters are expanding fastest. The projection captures a shift already visible in utility earnings and grid planning: power availability, not chip supply, is increasingly the constraint that determines how fast hyperscalers can bring new AI capacity online. Utilities in PJM territory have flagged multiyear queues for new large-load interconnections, and grid operators warn that demand growth of this scale requires new generation and transmission capacity, and in some cases, direct on-site power deals that bypass the public grid entirely.
trump-eu-301-investigation-bigtech-fines: President Trump announced the US has opened a Section 301 investigation into what he calls the European Union's practice of "robbing" American companies through antitrust fines, and threatened a "substantial tariff" on the EU in response. In a Truth Social post, Trump listed the EU's recent penalties: $15 billion against Apple, $3 billion against Meta, $2.5 billion against Amazon, and, just announced, another $1 billion against Google, which he said brings Google's cumulative EU fines above $18 billion. He called the fines "illegal and highly discriminatory," said they began under the Biden administration, and pledged the practice "is not going to continue during the Trump Administration." Section 301 is a US trade law tool that lets the president investigate a foreign government's practices and, if found unfair, impose retaliatory tariffs without new legislation, the same authority Trump has used against China and other trading partners. He gave no specific tariff rate or timeline, saying only that penalties on US companies "will be entirely reversed" and a tariff is expected "at the earliest possible moment." The EU has used antitrust enforcement against US tech giants for years under its Digital Markets Act and general competition rules, arguing the fines address anticompetitive conduct rather than target American firms specifically.
jensen-open-models-letter: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang posted on X for the first time on July 24th, using the debut to share a letter Nvidia signed arguing that open AI models deserve as much support as closed, proprietary ones. The letter states that AI will transform every industry, power every company, and eventually be built by every country, and argues open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, speed up innovation and its spread to more users, and let countries build AI systems under their own control rather than depending entirely on foreign providers. Huang's post frames the choice between open and closed models as false, saying the world needs both kinds of frontier systems rather than picking one over the other. The full letter is posted as a PDF on Nvidia's own site. Huang's move comes as Nvidia, whose GPUs power most AI training and inference worldwide, has increasingly positioned itself as a backer of open-weight models such as Meta's Llama family, even as it also profits from closed labs like OpenAI and Anthropic buying its chips. Taking a public stance now lands in the middle of an active policy fight in Washington and Beijing over whether open-source AI helps or threatens national security, a debate that could shape future export rules and government AI contracts.
kobeissi-ai-capex-sox-correlation-collap: The stock market is starting to treat AI chipmakers and AI spenders as two separate trades instead of one, The Kobeissi Letter reports. The 30-day correlation between the largest US capital-expenditure spenders on AI infrastructure and the semiconductor index, the SOX, has fallen to near zero, the lowest reading in at least four and a half years. That's down sharply from +0.78 in April, and well below the +0.60 average correlation since the start of 2022. Since early June the two groups have moved in opposite directions: semiconductor stocks have rallied even as the biggest AI infrastructure spenders, the hyperscalers pouring hundreds of billions into data centers, have declined, and the pattern has also run in reverse on other days. Kobeissi reads the split as a sign that investors no longer see AI chip demand and AI infrastructure spending as a single story that rises and falls together. Chipmakers keep benefiting from AI demand regardless of who is paying for it, while hyperscalers face growing questions about whether their spending will generate enough revenue to justify the cost. Kobeissi's conclusion is that the next phase of the AI trade will be judged on profitability rather than on how much companies are willing to spend.
netinterest-stripe-paypal-bid: Stripe and private equity firm Advent have offered to acquire PayPal for around $53 billion, Net Interest's Marc Rubinstein reports, with the deal reportedly structured so Stripe and Advent would each own half of PayPal, backed by $50 billion in committed bank financing. The offer follows a secondary tender offer that valued Stripe itself at $159 billion, and it closes a loop that started in 2013, when PayPal, then still owned by eBay, tried to buy Stripe outright and was turned down by founders Patrick and John Collison. PayPal instead bought Braintree, the maker of Venmo, for $800 million, but over the following decade Stripe's payment volume compounded at 70% a year against Braintree's 43%. Last year Stripe processed $1.9 trillion in payments to Braintree's $600 billion. PayPal, meanwhile, has churned through three CEOs in three years and a string of missteps since. Rubinstein frames the central question as why Stripe, now the clear winner of that old rivalry, wants to buy the company it once tried to escape, and whether $53 billion is close to the right price, a question his fuller analysis addresses beyond this preview.
kobeissi-oracle-cds-record: Oracle's cost of insuring against a default has hit a record, with five-year credit default swaps trading near 203 basis points, meaning investors now pay roughly $203,000 a year to insure $10 million of the company's debt against non-payment, The Kobeissi Letter reports. That level has more than quadrupled since mid-2025 and now sits above where Oracle's CDS traded at the peak of the 2008 financial crisis. The stress shows up in the bond market too. Oracle's 6.7% notes due 2056 widened 8 basis points this week to a 263 basis point spread over Treasurys, and its 5.7% notes due 2036 widened 9 basis points to 205. S&P Global Ratings downgraded Oracle to BBB-, one notch above junk, on July 9th, citing the company's fast-growing spending on AI data centers. Oracle has taken on debt at an unusual pace to build out cloud capacity for AI customers including OpenAI, and investors are increasingly pricing in the risk that revenue from those contracts doesn't arrive fast enough to cover the bill. A further downgrade to junk status would raise Oracle's borrowing costs even more and could trigger selling by funds that only hold investment-grade debt.
jukan-samsung-hynix-silicon-valley-deal: Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are expected to sign “very large-scale” supply contracts with major US technology companies during President Lee Jae-myung's upcoming trip to Silicon Valley, Kim Yong-beom, the presidential chief of staff for policy, said, according to semiconductor analyst Jukan. Kim, a career financial regulator who now leads the economic side of Lee's policy team, did not name which US companies are involved or specify whether the deals cover memory chips, foundry work, or both. The trip comes as Korea's two memory giants race to lock in customers for HBM4, the next generation of high-bandwidth memory that feeds AI accelerators. Samsung is still working to close a definitive supply agreement with AMD, while SK hynix is defending its position as Nvidia's main HBM supplier. A presidential-level announcement would put Seoul's diplomatic weight behind commercial contracts that are normally negotiated privately between companies, a sign of how central memory chip exports have become to Korea's economic relationship with Washington.
jukan-amd-samsung-hbm4-deal: AMD is on the verge of signing a definitive agreement with Samsung Electronics for large-scale supply of HBM4, the newest generation of high-bandwidth memory that sits next to AI chips and feeds them data at high speed, semiconductor analyst Jukan reports. At AMD's Advancing AI 2026 event in San Francisco, CEO Lisa Su was asked whether a substantive supply agreement was coming after the two companies signed a memorandum of understanding for priority HBM4 supply back in March. Her answer: "We're almost there." The signal was reinforced by who showed up: Samsung sent the head of its foundry division and the executive running its US semiconductor operations to the event, and the two stayed through Su's entire two-hour keynote before continuing talks with AMD's senior executives afterward. Su also said AMD's Helios AI server racks are now in full production and set to start shipping at the end of the third quarter, which raises the stakes on locking down HBM4 supply in time. For Samsung, landing a major HBM4 customer beyond Nvidia would mark real progress in its attempt to close the gap with SK hynix in advanced memory, a race it has been losing since the AI boom began. Samsung executives declined to comment directly, citing an "important meeting coming up shortly," but the body language, and Su's own words, point toward an announcement that isn't far off.
jukan-chip-equipment-lead-times-double: Lead times for the machines that build chips have stretched by 1.5 to 2 times in recent months, and equipment that once shipped in six months can now take a full year to arrive, industry sources say. The bottleneck traces back to simultaneous fab investment by chipmakers worldwide, all racing to add capacity for AI-driven demand, which has caused orders to pile up faster than the five biggest equipment makers, Applied Materials, ASML, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron and KLA, together controlling about 70% of the global market, can fill them. The strain isn't limited to those giants either. Korean suppliers feeding TSMC and Micron report their own lead times stretching from three to four months out to six to eight months, with some equipment now taking over a year. In response, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, both mid-construction on multiple new fabs, are said to be placing purchase orders earlier than usual to avoid getting stuck at the back of the queue. Unlike the equipment shortage of 2021 and 2022, which was driven by pandemic-era logistics chaos, this one stems purely from the scale of fab investment itself, and industry officials expect delivery times to keep stretching as chipmakers everywhere continue expanding. The risk is that fabs planned by Samsung and SK hynix could open later than scheduled if the machines they need don't show up on time, turning a supply-chain footnote into a real constraint on how fast memory and logic capacity can grow.
